answer_concept.name: A Regular Hexagon from Six Triangles: Ans1

item.question: Angles of 40°, 60°, 50°, 30°, 40° and 90° are placed round a point O, leaving a gap ∠AOI. Find the gap angle. Will a 70° angle fit into the gap?
steps_tex: All the angles round a point add up to $360^\circ$.
$40^\circ + 60^\circ + 50^\circ + 30^\circ + 40^\circ + 90^\circ +$ gap angle $= 360^\circ$.
The six known angles add to $310^\circ$.
So the gap angle is $360^\circ - 310^\circ = 50^\circ$.
$70^\circ$ is more than $50^\circ$, so the $70^\circ$ angle would overlap its neighbours.
item.answer_tex: The gap is $50^\circ$, so the $70^\circ$ angle does not fit
steps: All the angles round a point add up to 360°.
The six known angles add to 310°.
So the gap angle is 360° − 310° = 50°.
70° is more than 50°, so the 70° angle would overlap its neighbours.
item.answer: The gap is 50°, so the 70° angle does not fit
item.text:
$1$. All the angles round a point add up to $360^\circ$.
$2$. $40^\circ + 60^\circ + 50^\circ + 30^\circ + 40^\circ + 90^\circ +$ gap angle $= 360^\circ$.
$3$. The six known angles add to $310^\circ$.
$4$. So the gap angle is $360^\circ - 310^\circ = 50^\circ$.
$5$. $70^\circ$ is more than $50^\circ$, so the $70^\circ$ angle would overlap its neighbours.
Answer: The gap is $50^\circ$, so the $70^\circ$ angle does not fit

answer_concept.name: A Regular Hexagon from Six Triangles: Ans2

item.question: In a regular hexagon ABCDEF made of six equilateral triangles round the centre O, explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines.
steps_tex: At $O$, $\angle AOB$, $\angle BOC$ and $\angle COD$ are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is $60^\circ$.
$\angle AOD = \angle AOB + \angle BOC + \angle COD = 60^\circ + 60^\circ + 60^\circ = 180^\circ$.
An angle of $180^\circ$ is a straight angle, so $OA$ and $OD$ point in opposite directions: $AOD$ is a straight line.
In the same way $\angle BOE = 180^\circ$ and $\angle COF = 180^\circ$.
So $BOE$ and $COF$ are straight lines too.
item.answer_tex: Each of $\angle AOD$, $\angle BOE$ and $\angle COF$ is three $60^\circ$ angles, which is $180^\circ$, a straight angle
steps: At O, ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠COD are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is 60°.
An angle of 180° is a straight angle, so OA and OD point in opposite directions: AOD is a straight line.
In the same way ∠BOE = 180° and ∠COF = 180°.
So BOE and COF are straight lines too.
item.answer: Each of ∠AOD, ∠BOE and ∠COF is three 60° angles, which is 180°, a straight angle
item.text:
$1$. At $O$, $\angle AOB$, $\angle BOC$ and $\angle COD$ are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is $60^\circ$.
$2$. $\angle AOD = \angle AOB + \angle BOC + \angle COD = 60^\circ + 60^\circ + 60^\circ = 180^\circ$.
$3$. An angle of $180^\circ$ is a straight angle, so $OA$ and $OD$ point in opposite directions: $AOD$ is a straight line.
$4$. In the same way $\angle BOE = 180^\circ$ and $\angle COF = 180^\circ$.
$5$. So $BOE$ and $COF$ are straight lines too.
Answer: Each of $\angle AOD$, $\angle BOE$ and $\angle COF$ is three $60^\circ$ angles, which is $180^\circ$, a straight angle

concept_name: 120° and regular hexagons of a given side

item.question: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: Draw a line and mark A on it. Mark X on the line to the right of A.
With centre A and any radius, draw a large arc that cuts AX at B.
With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60°.
With centre C and the same radius, cut the arc again at D. Then ∠DAC = 60°, by the same equilateral triangle reason.
Join A and D. ∠DAX = 60° + 60° = 120°.
Check: D lies on the side away from X, and the angle between AD and the line on the left is 180° − 120° = 60°.
item.answer: ∠DAX = 120°, made of two 60° angles from equilateral triangles
item.text:
Worked example: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
1. Draw a line and mark A on it. Mark X on the line to the right of A.
2. With centre A and any radius, draw a large arc that cuts AX at B.
3. With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60°.
4. With centre C and the same radius, cut the arc again at D. Then ∠DAC = 60°, by the same equilateral triangle reason.
5. Join A and D. ∠DAX = 60° + 60° = 120°.
6. Check: D lies on the side away from X, and the angle between AD and the line on the left is 180° − 120° = 60°.
Answer: ∠DAX = 120°, made of two 60° angles from equilateral triangles

item.question: Construct a regular hexagon with side 4 cm using a ruler and a compass.
steps_tex: Open the compass to $4\text{ cm}$ using the ruler, and draw a circle with centre $O$.
Mark a point $A$ on the circle.
With centre $A$ and radius $4\text{ cm}$, cut the circle at $B$. $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral, so $\angle AOB = 60^\circ$.
With centre $B$, cut the circle at $C$; with centre $C$, cut at $D$; then $E$ and $F$ in the same way.
Six angles of $60^\circ$ at $O$ make $360^\circ$, so the sixth step lands back on $A$.
Join $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ in order. Every side is $4\text{ cm}$ and every angle is $60^\circ + 60^\circ = 120^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: $ABCDEF$, with six sides of $4\text{ cm}$ and six angles of $120^\circ$
steps: Open the compass to 4 cm using the ruler, and draw a circle with centre O.
Mark a point A on the circle.
With centre A and radius 4 cm, cut the circle at B. ΔOAB is equilateral, so ∠AOB = 60°.
With centre B, cut the circle at C; with centre C, cut at D; then E and F in the same way.
Six angles of 60° at O make 360°, so the sixth step lands back on A.
Join A, B, C, D, E, F in order. Every side is 4 cm and every angle is 60° + 60° = 120°.
item.answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 4 cm and six angles of 120°
item.text:

$2$. Mark a point $A$ on the circle.
$3$. With centre $A$ and radius $4\text{ cm}$, cut the circle at $B$. $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral, so $\angle AOB = 60^\circ$.
$4$. With centre $B$, cut the circle at $C$; with centre $C$, cut at $D$; then $E$ and $F$ in the same way.
$5$. Six angles of $60^\circ$ at $O$ make $360^\circ$, so the sixth step lands back on $A$.
$6$. Join $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ in order. Every side is $4\text{ cm}$ and every angle is $60^\circ + 60^\circ = 120^\circ$.
Answer: $ABCDEF$, with six sides of $4\text{ cm}$ and six angles of $120^\circ$

item.question: Construct a 60° angle at A on a segment AX using only a ruler and a compass, and explain why it is 60°.
steps_tex: With centre $A$ and any radius, draw a long arc that cuts $AX$ at $B$.
With centre $B$ and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the first arc at $C$.
Join $A$ and $C$. $\angle CAX$ is the required angle.
Join $B$ and $C$. $AB = AC$, because both are radii of the first arc.
$BA = BC$, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
So $AB = BC = CA$: $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral, and each of its angles is $60^\circ$. So $\angle CAX = 60^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: $\angle CAX = 60^\circ$, because $\triangle ABC$ has three equal sides and so is equilateral
steps: With centre A and any radius, draw a long arc that cuts AX at B.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the first arc at C.
Join A and C. ∠CAX is the required angle.
Join B and C. AB = AC, because both are radii of the first arc.
BA = BC, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
So AB = BC = CA: ΔABC is equilateral, and each of its angles is 60°. So ∠CAX = 60°.
item.answer: ∠CAX = 60°, because ΔABC has three equal sides and so is equilateral
item.text:
$1$. With centre $A$ and any radius, draw a long arc that cuts $AX$ at $B$.
$2$. With centre $B$ and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the first arc at $C$.
$3$. Join $A$ and $C$. $\angle CAX$ is the required angle.
$4$. Join $B$ and $C$. $AB = AC$, because both are radii of the first arc.
$5$. $BA = BC$, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
$6$. So $AB = BC = CA$: $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral, and each of its angles is $60^\circ$. So $\angle CAX = 60^\circ$.
Answer: $\angle CAX = 60^\circ$, because $\triangle ABC$ has three equal sides and so is equilateral

item.question: Construct a regular hexagon with side 5 cm using the 120° construction at each corner.
steps_tex: Draw $AB = 5\text{ cm}$ with the ruler.
At $B$, construct $120^\circ$ between $BA$ and a new ray: two $60^\circ$ steps with equal arcs. Cut the ray at $C$ with $BC = 5\text{ cm}$.
At $C$, construct $120^\circ$ in the same way, turning the same direction, and cut $CD = 5\text{ cm}$.
Repeat at $D$ and $E$ to get $E$ and $F$ with $DE = EF = 5\text{ cm}$.
Join $F$ to $A$. The angles of a regular hexagon add to $6 \times 120 = 720$ degrees, and $FA$ comes out $5\text{ cm}$.
All six sides are $5\text{ cm}$ and all six angles are $120^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: $ABCDEF$, with six sides of $5\text{ cm}$ and six angles of $120^\circ$
steps: Draw AB = 5 cm with the ruler.
At B, construct 120° between BA and a new ray: two 60° steps with equal arcs. Cut the ray at C with BC = 5 cm.
At C, construct 120° in the same way, turning the same direction, and cut CD = 5 cm.
Repeat at D and E to get E and F with DE = EF = 5 cm.
Join F to A. The angles of a regular hexagon add to 6 × 120 = 720 degrees, and FA comes out 5 cm.
All six sides are 5 cm and all six angles are 120°.
item.answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 5 cm and six angles of 120°

item.question: Construct a 30° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
steps_tex: With centre $A$ and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the line at $B$.
With centre $B$ and the same radius, cut the arc at $C$. Then $\angle CAB = 60^\circ$, because $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral.
Now bisect $\angle CAB$: with one radius, draw arcs from $B$ and from $C$ that meet at $D$ inside the angle.
Join $A$ and $D$.
$AB = AC$, $BD = CD$ and $AD$ is common, so $\triangle ABD$ is congruent to $\triangle ACD$ by $SSS$.
So $\angle DAB = \angle DAC$, and each is half of $60^\circ$, which is $30^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: $\angle DAB = 30^\circ$: a $60^\circ$ angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected using $SSS$
steps: With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the line at B.
With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60° (ΔABC is equilateral).
Now bisect ∠CAB: with one radius, draw arcs from B and from C that meet at D inside the angle.
Join A and D.
AB = AC, BD = CD and AD is common, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS.
So ∠DAB = ∠DAC, and each is half of 60°, which is 30°.
item.answer: ∠DAB = 30°: a 60° angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected (SSS)

$3$. Now bisect $\angle CAB$: with one radius, draw arcs from $B$ and from $C$ that meet at $D$ inside the angle.
$4$. Join $A$ and $D$.
$5$. $AB = AC$, $BD = CD$ and $AD$ is common, so $\triangle ABD$ is congruent to $\triangle ACD$ by $SSS$.
$6$. So $\angle DAB = \angle DAC$, and each is half of $60^\circ$, which is $30^\circ$.
Answer: $\angle DAB = 30^\circ$: a $60^\circ$ angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected using $SSS$

extra_items.question: Construct a 15° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
steps_tex: Construct $\angle CAB = 60^\circ$ with two equal arcs, and bisect it to get the ray $AD$ with $\angle DAB = 30^\circ$.
The first arc from $A$ cuts $AD$ at a point $E$. Then $AB = AE$.
With one radius, draw arcs from $B$ and from $E$ that meet at $F$ inside $\angle DAB$.
Join $A$ and $F$.
$AB = AE$, $BF = EF$ and $AF$ is common, so $\triangle ABF$ is congruent to $\triangle AEF$ by $SSS$.
So $\angle FAB$ is half of $30^\circ$, which is $15^\circ$.

item.question: A six-pointed star has outer points A, B, C, D, E, F and an inner regular hexagon GHIJKL. Are the six point triangles ΔAGH, ΔBHI, ΔCIJ, ΔDJK, ΔELK and ΔFLG equilateral? Why?
steps_tex: The inner figure $GHIJKL$ is a regular hexagon, so each of its angles is $120^\circ$.
In $\triangle AGH$, side $GH$ is a side of the hexagon, and $AG$ and $AH$ lie along the extended sides $LG$ and $IH$.
$\angle AGH$ and $\angle LGH$ make a straight angle, so $\angle AGH = 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
In the same way $\angle AHG = 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle GAH = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 60^\circ = 60^\circ$.
All three angles are $60^\circ$, so $\triangle AGH$ is equilateral; the same reasoning works for the other five points.
item.answer_tex: Yes. Each base angle is $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$, so all three angles are $60^\circ$ and each point is an equilateral triangle

item.question: Draw a line l and mark a point P anywhere outside the line. Construct a perpendicular to the given line l through P. [Hint: Find a line segment on l whose perpendicular bisector passes through P.]
steps_tex: With centre $P$ and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts $l$ at two points $X$ and $Y$. Then $PX = PY$.
$P$ is equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $XY$.
With centres $X$ and $Y$ and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of $l$ that meet at $Q$. Then $QX = QY$.
Join $P$ and $Q$; $PQ$ meets $l$ at $O$.
$\triangle PXQ$ is congruent to $\triangle PYQ$ by $SSS$, so $\angle XPO = \angle YPO$; then $\triangle POX$ is congruent to $\triangle POY$ by $SAS$, so $\angle POX = \angle POY = 90^\circ$.
So $PQ$ is the perpendicular to $l$ through $P$.
item.answer_tex: Cut $l$ at $X$ and $Y$ with an arc from $P$, then find $Q$ with $QX = QY$; $PQ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $XY$, using $SSS$ and then $SAS$, so it is perpendicular to $l$ and passes through $P$
steps: With centre P and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts l at two points X and Y. Then PX = PY.
P is equally far from X and Y, so P lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
With centres X and Y and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of l that meet at Q. Then QX = QY.
Join P and Q; PQ meets l at O.
ΔPXQ ≅ ΔPYQ by SSS, so ∠XPO = ∠YPO; then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS, so ∠POX = ∠POY = 90°.
So PQ is the perpendicular to l through P.
item.answer: Cut l at X and Y with an arc from P, then find Q with QX = QY; PQ is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS), so it is perpendicular to l and passes through P
item.text:
$1$. With centre $P$ and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts $l$ at two points $X$ and $Y$. Then $PX = PY$.
$2$. $P$ is equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $XY$.
$3$. With centres $X$ and $Y$ and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of $l$ that meet at $Q$. Then $QX = QY$.
$4$. Join $P$ and $Q$; $PQ$ meets $l$ at $O$.
$5$. $\triangle PXQ$ is congruent to $\triangle PYQ$ by $SSS$, so $\angle XPO = \angle YPO$; then $\triangle POX$ is congruent to $\triangle POY$ by $SAS$, so $\angle POX = \angle POY = 90^\circ$.
$6$. So $PQ$ is the perpendicular to $l$ through $P$.
Answer: Cut $l$ at $X$ and $Y$ with an arc from $P$, then find $Q$ with $QX = QY$; $PQ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $XY$, using $SSS$ and then $SAS$, so it is perpendicular to $l$ and passes through $P$

item.question: Prove that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
steps_tex: The grid has $5 \times 7 = 35$ squares of side $1\text{ unit}$.
Each tile covers exactly $2$ squares of side $1\text{ unit}$, with no overlap.
So any number of tiles covers an even number of squares.
$35$ is odd, so it is not a number of squares that tiles can cover exactly.
So there is no tiling of the $5 \times 7$ grid.

An odd number times an odd number is odd, for example $3 \times 5 = 15$.
Each tile covers $2$ squares, so tiles always cover an even number of squares.
An odd number of squares can never be covered exactly.
